analysis.one_liner: Creates a public, searchable database of corporate crimes and federal enforcement outcomes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to two House committees in December 2023 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would order the Bureau of Justice Statistics to build a public website listing federal enforcement actions against companies and their executives — including settlements and cases where prosecutors declined to act — naming the company, its parent company, the alleged offense, and the outcome. It would also require an annual report to Congress on corporate crime, repeat offenders, and the harm to victims, with recommendations for better enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who deal with companies as workers, customers, investors, or neighbors gain a free way to check a company's record of federal violations — including quiet settlements and declined prosecutions that today are scattered across agency websites or not published at all. Researchers, journalists, and regulators would also gain a single comprehensive dataset.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, workers, and investors checking companies

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Bureau of Justice Statistics to publish, within one year, a searchable, downloadable public database of federal enforcement actions for corporate offenses, including settlements, deferred- and non-prosecution agreements, and declinations — the cases where an agency looked at a company and chose not to act.

The database must name each business entity and individual, the individual's employer, and the parent company, along with the statute or regulation violated, the agency bringing the action, and all documentation of the outcome — making it possible to track a corporation's record across all federal agencies in one place.

Requires an annual report to Congress analyzing repeat offenders and the estimated impact of corporate offenses on victims and the public, with recommendations to improve federal monitoring and deterrence.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations and their executives would bear the cost of having their federal enforcement records — including matters resolved quietly or not at all — consolidated and published for the public to search. Federal agencies would shoulder the work of collecting and submitting the data.

drawbacks.text: The database lists alleged violations as well as adjudicated ones, so a company could appear in the database based on an accusation that was never proven or was later settled without admission of wrongdoing; a 'declination' entry could stigmatize a firm that agencies cleared without charge.

The bill mandates data collection and publication by federal agencies but provides no funding mechanism in its text, and building a government-wide reporting system for enforcement actions would take sustained administrative effort and appropriations to work well.

A transparency database informs the public but changes no penalties, closes no legal loopholes, and does not itself make enforcement more aggressive; its value depends on agencies actually enforcing the underlying laws.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but indirect: a single, searchable record of corporate wrongdoing helps people make informed choices and helps journalists and researchers spot repeat offenders, at modest cost to agencies and some reputational exposure for companies. The main design risk is that listing mere allegations alongside proven violations could be unfair to individual firms, and the bill does nothing to change how corporations are actually punished.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in December 2023 and referred to the House Judiciary and Oversight committees, neither of which ever took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon introduced the Corporate Crime Database Act of 2023 on December 11, 2023, with seven Democratic cosponsors.

The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, additionally, to the Committee on Oversight and Accountability — the standard first step that sends a bill to committees with jurisdiction over its subject matter.

No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action. Because the bill was introduced in the first session of a two-year Congress and received no action in either session, it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Bills are not carried over between Congresses, so the bill would have to be reintroduced from scratch to have any chance of becoming law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies with federal enforcement records — including deferred-prosecution agreements, settlements, and cases agencies declined to pursue — are better off, because the consolidated public record that would have exposed their track record in one place was never created. The committees that never acted on the bill also avoided taking a recorded position on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies with enforcement records; the committees that sat on it

industries.industry: Corporations and business entities under federal enforcement
industries.note: The bill would consolidate every federal enforcement action against a company — including quiet settlements and declined prosecutions — into one public, searchable database naming parent companies and executives. Today this information is fragmented across agency websites, and declinations are often not published at all, so a public record is a direct reputational cost to firms with violations.

Agencies would take on new mandatory data-reporting duties and their enforcement records would become publicly comparable across agencies, but the annual report's deterrence recommendations could also support their enforcement work.
